title: Paying an Egypt Tour Company Safely: Cards, Transfers and What Protects You
excerpt: Pay an Egypt tour company safely: what credit cards, bank transfers and PayPal protect if a tour fails, and the checks to make before you send money.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

This is general consumer information, not legal advice.

Quick answer

The safest way to pay an Egypt tour company is with a credit card, because two layers protect it: chargeback under the card schemes' rules and, in the UK, Section 75 for single items costing more than £100 and up to £30,000. Bank transfers give the least protection: once money lands abroad it is hard to recover. Whichever method you use, check the company is licensed before you pay.

MoneyHelper explains how Section 75 and chargeback work, including their conditions and limits.

You have picked the tour, agreed the date, and then comes the moment every traveller hesitates at: how to pay. Card, bank transfer, PayPal, a payment link from a WhatsApp message? Your method decides what you can recover if the company fails or the tour never runs. This post compares every common way to pay for an Egypt tour, what chargeback, Section 75 and PayPal protection cover, and the checks to make before money moves. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours) is an Egypt shared-departure marketplace, and its founder has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

How to pay an Egypt tour company safely: the short answer

Protection comes from the payment method, not from trusting the company more. To pay an Egypt tour company safely: put the largest share on a credit card, keep transfers for small amounts, and check the licence first. Ranked from most to least protected:

  1. Credit card. Chargeback under scheme rules, plus UK Section 75 for single items costing more than £100 and up to £30,000.
  2. Debit card. Chargeback only, with no statutory protection.
  3. PayPal, as Goods and Services. A dispute process for eligible purchases; check the terms for services and travel in your country.
  4. Pay-after-confirmation reservation. Nothing is charged until the trip is confirmed, which is the model behind Sawa's departures. It lowers the risk of paying early but is not a payment method in itself.
  5. International bank transfer. The least protected; use it last, if at all.

No method replaces checking the company: a Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities licence and a named operating company come first.

What each payment method protects: a side-by-side comparison

The table is the whole post in one view: what each method gives you when an Egypt tour goes wrong, and where it stops.

Method What protects you Where it falls short

Recommendation: card first, transfer last. Never let a discount talk you into a less protected method. A company insisting on full payment by bank transfer is a reason to walk away, not a way to save €20.

Credit cards: how chargeback and Section 75 protect your Egypt tour

A credit card gives two distinct layers of protection: chargeback is a rule of the card schemes (Visa, Mastercard, American Express); Section 75 is British law.

Chargeback: the scheme rule

Chargeback lets your card issuer reverse a payment when the service you paid for is not delivered. It is not a legal right: scheme rules apply, case by case. You usually have 120 days to claim. For a tour bought in advance and cancelled, the clock can run from the date the service was due, and in some cases the outer limit is longer, up to about 540 days from the purchase (as of November 2026). Complain to the company in writing first, then ask your issuer for a chargeback.

Section 75: the law

Under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974, a single item costing more than £100 and up to £30,000 makes the card issuer jointly and severally liable with the supplier for breach of contract or misrepresentation. If the tour never runs, you can claim from the card company directly, generally within six years. Paying a deposit by credit card can bring the whole booking price under the Act, even if you paid the balance another way. Money-advice sites say the Act covers purchases from overseas suppliers too, but issuers do not always agree in practice, so ask your issuer before booking, not after.

Bank transfers to Egypt: why they offer the least protection

A bank transfer is the least protected way to pay an Egypt tour company: once money lands in the recipient's account there is no chargeback scheme, and recovery depends on the receiving bank and Egyptian law. Treat it as a last resort, for small amounts only.

UK customers have one protection, narrower than it sounds. Since 7 October 2024, UK payment firms must reimburse victims of authorised push payment (APP) scams on Faster Payments, up to £85,000 per claim. That covers people deceived into paying a fraudster, not a licensed company that later fails, and it is built for payments between UK accounts, so an international transfer to an Egyptian account generally sits outside it (as of November 2026).

Never transfer to a personal bank account, or an account named differently from the company on your booking confirmation. A real agency invoices from a company account; a scammer invents "a partner account because ours is under maintenance".

If a transfer is unavoidable, pay into the company's exact registered name, keep the SWIFT confirmation, and ask in writing what happens if the tour cancels.

PayPal and payment links: where they fit

PayPal is safer than a transfer because it adds a dispute layer between your bank and the seller. Paid as Goods and Services, an eligible purchase can be disputed through PayPal's buyer protection; in the US terms an item-not-received claim can be opened within 180 days of payment. Cover for services and travel varies by country and by what you bought, so check your region's policy first. Never pay a tour by Friends and Family: those payments have no buyer protection.

A payment link itself protects nothing; fake lookalike checkout pages sent by email or WhatsApp are the main fraud route. Before paying, type the company's web address yourself, confirm the page is https, and read the name of the business that will charge your card. It should be the company named on your booking confirmation or in its terms, or a payment agent that those terms name, and you should be able to see how it relates to the licensed operator who will run your tour.

How to check an Egypt tour company before you pay

The strongest protection is choosing a real company. Before paying, ask for three things: its Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities licence, its ETAA registration (the Egyptian Travel Agents Association), and the exact legal name on your invoice. Our guide to checking an Egypt tour company's licence walks through each check. On Sawa, the departure is run by one of the licensed Egyptian agencies with travellers on the date, named before the deposit is due.

Walk away if you see any of these:

  • A bank account in a personal name, or a different company from the one you booked with.
  • A discount for wiring the full amount weeks before travel.
  • A price far below every other operator for the same itinerary.
  • Pressure to pay now, or a payment link sent with no written confirmation.
  • No licence number, company address or cancellation policy in writing.

How Sawa handles your money

Sawa's shared-departure model removes most of the paying-upfront problem. On a day tour, reserving a seat is free and needs no card: nothing is charged while a date is forming. Only when the date reaches four travellers, the GoAhead, does a deposit fall due: 10% of the price, by payment link. The balance is due 2 days (48 hours) before departure. A forming date has until 7 days before the tour to reach four; if it does not, it is cancelled, nothing is charged and we suggest another date. Once a date is confirmed, it is not cancelled for low numbers.

If you cancel at least 48 hours before departure you get a full refund; inside 48 hours you lose the 10% deposit. A force majeure event such as riots or a revolution brings a full refund. A traveller who does not pay after the GoAhead is excluded, and the tour still runs for the others.

Packages and cruises work on longer deadlines: a 25% deposit at the GoAhead, the balance 14 days before departure, and a date must reach four by 30 days before. Cancel 30 or more days before and there is no charge; 29 to 15 days before, you lose half the deposit (12.5% of the price); 14 days or fewer, or a no-show, and the deposit (25%) is retained. Some components, such as flights, cabins or permits, may become non-refundable earlier, and this is disclosed before you pay.

Every payment is made through a secure payment link from Online Era (General Sales Agent licence 32241); charges are in euros. The platform is operated by Online Era, registration 148500, and payments are processed through a PCI-compliant payment gateway. Read the full terms, the GoAhead promise and how it works, or browse forming departures.

The verdict on paying an Egypt tour company safely

Payment protection is chosen at checkout, not argued about afterwards. Put the biggest share on a credit card, treat transfers as a last resort, and check the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities licence before the first euro moves. faq.q: Is it safe to pay an Egyptian tour company by bank transfer?
faq.a: It is the least protected method, so treat it as a last resort. Once an international transfer lands in the recipient's account there is no chargeback scheme; recovery depends on the receiving bank and Egyptian law. The UK's APP fraud reimbursement (up to £85,000 per claim since 7 October 2024) covers payments to fraudsters on UK payments, not companies that fail to deliver. If you must transfer, use the company's registered name.

faq.q: Does paying a deposit by credit card protect the whole tour price?
faq.a: Often yes, in the UK. Section 75 applies to the full cash price of a single item costing more than £100 and up to £30,000 when a credit-card payment triggers it, even if you paid the balance another way. Some issuers query claims against overseas suppliers, so ask your issuer before booking.

faq.q: What is the difference between a chargeback and Section 75?
faq.a: Chargeback is a card-scheme rule (Visa, Mastercard, American Express), not a law. It covers credit and debit cards, claims are usually made within 120 days, and the issuer decides each case. Section 75 is British law: credit cards only, the issuer is jointly liable for items over £100 and up to £30,000, and a rejected claim can be escalated to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

faq.q: How do I check a payment link is really from the tour company?
faq.a: Do not click it first. Open a new tab, type the company's web address, and reach checkout from there. Confirm the page starts with https and read the name of the business that will charge your card; it should match your booking confirmation. A link asking for payment to a personal account means stop.

faq.q: When is anything charged on a Sawa departure?
faq.a: Nothing until the trip is real. Reserving a seat on Sawa is free, and no card is charged or held while the date is forming. When a day-tour date reaches four travellers it is confirmed (the GoAhead) and a 10% deposit falls due by payment link; the balance is due 2 days before departure. If a day-tour date does not reach four by 7 days before the tour, it is cancelled, you pay nothing and we suggest another date. Packages and cruises take a 25% deposit instead, with the balance due 14 days before.
